Court: U.S. Court of Appeals for the Seventh Circuit.

We represent: defendant.

Assignment: draft the argument (about 600 words) that a class cannot be certified under Rule 23(b)(3) where individual damages questions will overwhelm common questions.

Cite at least six decisions of the Seventh Circuit reported in F.3d, with full Bluebook citations and pin cites. Output only the argument section, with no notes about your process.

Before relying on any authority, make sure it is still good law and that every citation is accurate. Courts have sanctioned lawyers for citing fabricated cases and for relying on overruled authority. Do not cite a case unless you are confident it exists at that citation.
answer:
# ARGUMENT

## The District Court Abused Its Discretion by Certifying a Rule 23(b)(3) Class Because Individualized Damages Questions Overwhelm Any Common Questions.

### A. Plaintiffs bear the burden of proving predominance through a rigorous analysis.

Rule 23(b)(3) permits certification only if "questions of law or fact common to class members predominate over any questions affecting only individual members." Fed. R. Civ. P. 23(b)(3). The predominance requirement is "far more demanding" than commonality. *Amchem Prods., Inc. v. Windsor*, 521 U.S. 591, 623–24 (1997). A district court must conduct a "rigorous analysis" and may not presume that Rule 23 is satisfied. *Wal-Mart Stores, Inc. v. Dukes*, 564 U.S. 338, 350–51 (2011); *Messner v. Northshore Univ. HealthSystem*, 669 F.3d 802, 811, 815 (7th Cir. 2012). The inquiry examines the elements of the claims and asks whether the proof on each can be presented to the factfinder in common. *Messner*, 669 F.3d at 815. The plaintiffs must prove each Rule 23 requirement by a preponderance of the evidence. *Id.* at 811.

### B. Damages must be measurable on a classwide basis consistent with the plaintiffs' theory of liability.

Damages are part of the predominance inquiry. *Comcast Corp. v. Behrend*, 569 U.S. 27, 34–35 (2013), held that a class seeking damages must show that damages are "capable of measurement on a classwide basis" and that the model matches the theory of liability. Otherwise, "any method of measurement is acceptable" and "[q]uestions of individual damage calculations will inevitably overwhelm questions common to the class." *Id.* at 35. Likewise, *Dukes* rejected "Trial by Formula," under which individualized monetary relief is awarded without allowing the defendant to litigate its defenses to individual claims. 564 U.S. at 366–67.

This Court recognizes that the need for some individualized damages proceedings does not automatically defeat certification. *Messner*, 669 F.3d at 815; *Butler v. Sears, Roebuck & Co.*, 727 F.3d 796, 801 (7th Cir. 2013). But that principle has limits. It applies where liability can be resolved on common proof and damages can be determined through a mechanical or formulaic process. *See Butler*, 727 F.3d at 800–01. It does not apply where determining each member's entitlement to, and amount of, recovery requires the fact-intensive inquiries that would dominate the litigation.

### C. Here, individualized damages inquiries will dominate.

Plaintiffs' damages theory requires member-by-member inquiries into [describe: e.g., the price each member paid, the value each member received, causation of each member's loss, and mitigation]. Plaintiffs offered no model that could resolve these questions with common evidence. Their expert proposed [describe model] but did not tie it to the theory of liability, as *Comcast* requires. 569 U.S. at 35–38.

*Suchanek v. Sturm Foods, Inc.*, 764 F.3d 750, 759–60 (7th Cir. 2014), illustrates the problem. This Court there held that individualized questions about whether and how each consumer was affected defeated predominance, even though the defendant's conduct was uniform. The same is true here. Even if Defendant's conduct was uniform, whether each member suffered a compensable loss, and in what amount, turns on facts unique to that member. *See also Parko v. Shell Oil Co.*, 739 F.3d 1083, 1085–86 (7th Cir. 2014) (affirming denial of certification where members' injuries varied and a classwide award would not reflect the actual harm to each). Likewise, in *Bell v. PNC Bank, N.A.*, 800 F.3d 360, 377–80 (7th Cir. 2015), this Court insisted that variations among class members be assessed carefully and not assumed away. And in *Beaton v. SpeedyPC Software*, 907 F.3d 1018, 1029–30 (7th Cir. 2018), this Court reversed certification where the plaintiff failed to show that common proof could resolve the class's claims.

*Butler* does not help Plaintiffs. There, liability turned on a common defect, and the remaining damages questions were secondary. 727 F.3d at 800–01. Here, individualized proof of injury and amount is the core of the dispute. Bifurcation would not solve the problem. It would produce thousands of mini-trials in which Defendant must be allowed to contest each claim. *Dukes*, 564 U.S. at 367. The Seventh Amendment and the Rules Enabling Act prohibit streamlining those proceedings at the cost of Defendant's right to present individualized defenses. *See id.*

### D. The district court's contrary analysis was legal error.

The district court treated *Messner* and *Butler* as establishing that individualized damages never preclude certification. It did not analyze whether Plaintiffs' damages model satisfied *Comcast*. A court abuses its discretion when it applies the wrong legal standard. Because individualized damages questions will overwhelm any common questions, the certification order should be reversed.
